questions.question: What is Apache Maven and what is 'convention over configuration'?
questions.title: What Is Maven?
questions.direct_answer: Maven is a build automation and dependency management tool for Java projects that uses 'convention over configuration' — it defines standard directory layouts and build lifecycle phases so you follow conventions instead of writing custom build scripts. You get clean, compile, test, and package commands that just work without explicit configuration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Maven's design philosophy and can explain 'convention over configuration' — a core concept that appears in Spring Boot and modern Java frameworks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing Maven only as 'it manages dependencies' without mentioning the full build lifecycle or the convention principle that makes it different from Ant
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast Maven's opinionated conventions with Gradle's flexibility and explain when each approach is better — Maven for standard projects, Gradle when you need custom build logic

sections.title: Maven's Build Automation Philosophy
sections.content:
Apache Maven is a comprehensive build automation tool that manages the entire lifecycle of Java projects — from compiling source code to running tests to packaging deployable artifacts. Think of Maven like an assembly line in a car factory: every car goes through the same stations in the same order (welding, painting, assembly), and you don't need to design the process from scratch each time.

The **convention over configuration** principle means Maven provides sensible defaults for everything — your source code goes in src/main/java, tests in src/test/java, and built artifacts in target/. Instead of writing hundreds of lines of build scripts, you declare what your project needs in a single pom.xml file and Maven figures out the how. This dramatically reduces boilerplate and makes every Maven project immediately familiar to any Java developer. Maven executes a **build lifecycle** with predefined phases: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, and deploy.

sections.title: Maven at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Convention|~Standard layout|src/main/java|no custom scripts|every project looks alike
blue|Lifecycle|~Phases in order|validate to deploy|one command runs all|predictable builds
emerald|Dependencies|~Declarative|pom.xml coordinates|transitive resolution|from Maven Central
violet|Plugins|~Do the real work|compiler, surefire|spring-boot plugin|extend the lifecycle

sections.title: Minimal Maven Project Structure and pom.xml
sections.content:
```xml
// Minimal pom.xml for a Spring Boot application
<project>
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  
  <groupId>com.company.ecommerce</groupId>
  <artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0</version>
  <packaging>jar</packaging>
  
  <parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.2.0</version> // Inherits plugin configs and dependency versions
  </parent>
  
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
      // Version inherited from parent
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
  
  <build>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        // Creates executable jar with embedded Tomcat
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>
</project>
```

sections.title: When Maven's Conventions Shine
sections.content:
Use Maven when your project follows standard Java patterns and you want zero-configuration builds. **Enterprise Spring Boot applications** benefit enormously because Maven's conventions align perfectly with Spring's structure — no custom scripting needed for multi-module microservices. **Open-source libraries** almost always use Maven because publishing to Maven Central requires a pom.xml, and the ecosystem expects it. **Teams with junior developers** benefit from Maven's guardrails — there's one obvious way to do things, which prevents fragmentation.

Use Gradle instead when you need complex custom build logic, Android development, or polyglot projects mixing Java with Kotlin or Scala where Gradle's Groovy DSL provides more flexibility.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating Maven as just a dependency downloader**: Freshers often think Maven only fetches JARs from the internet and miss that it orchestrates the entire build lifecycle including compilation, testing, and packaging. This leads to confusion when mvn install does more than expected.
- **Fighting Maven's conventions unnecessarily**: New developers sometimes create custom src/code or src/classes directories instead of using src/main/java, then spend hours configuring Maven to recognize them. Follow the conventions — they exist for good reasons and every IDE understands them.
- **Not understanding the parent POM hierarchy**: Freshers declare spring-boot-starter-parent as a dependency instead of a parent, which breaks version management and plugin inheritance, causing cryptic build errors.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Convention over configuration**: Maven defines standard project layouts and build phases so you don't write custom scripts — just declare dependencies and goals
- **Build lifecycle**: Maven executes phases in order (clean → validate → compile → test → package → install → deploy) with each phase having pre-defined behavior
- **Declarative configuration**: The pom.xml file describes what your project is and what it needs — Maven figures out how to build it
- **Dependency management**: Maven automatically downloads libraries from Maven Central and resolves transitive dependencies without manual intervention
- **Plugin ecosystem**: Maven's functionality comes from plugins (compiler, surefire for tests, jar packager) that execute during lifecycle phases
- **Multi-module projects**: Maven excels at building projects with multiple sub-modules that depend on each other using reactor builds
- **IDE integration**: IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, and VS Code natively understand Maven projects and sync dependencies automatically

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven is a build automation tool for Java that manages dependencies and executes the full build lifecycle from compiling code to packaging deployable artifacts. The key idea is convention over configuration — Maven gives you standard directory layouts and build phases so you don't write custom scripts. For example, your Java source always goes in src slash main slash java and tests in src slash test slash java. When you run mvn package, Maven automatically compiles your code, runs tests, and creates a JAR file without you configuring those steps explicitly. This is different from older tools like Ant where you'd write hundreds of lines of XML to define every compilation step. In a Spring Boot project, you just declare spring-boot-starter-web in your pom dot XML, and Maven downloads not just that library but also all its transitive dependencies like Tomcat and Jackson. The convention approach means every Maven project looks the same, which is huge for team productivity. One common mistake freshers make is treating Maven as just a dependency downloader — it's actually orchestrating your entire build process. If you need lots of custom build logic or non-Java languages, you might choose Gradle instead, but for standard Java backend work, Maven's conventions eliminate a ton of boilerplate.

questions.question: What are Maven coordinates and what do groupId, artifactId, and version mean?
questions.title: Maven Coordinates: groupId, artifactId, version (GAV)
questions.direct_answer: Maven coordinates are the unique identifier for any artifact in the Maven ecosystem, written as groupId:artifactId:version (GAV). The groupId is the organization or package namespace like org.springframework, the artifactId is the specific module name like spring-core, and the version is the release number like 5.3.31.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Maven fluency — GAV coordinates appear in every pom.xml dependency declaration and are essential for dependency resolution
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing groupId with package name or not understanding that groupId prevents naming collisions between different organizations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Maven coordinates solve the namespace collision problem — two organizations can publish artifacts with the same artifactId as long as their groupIds differ, like com.google.guava:guava vs com.github.ben-manes.caffeine:caffeine

sections.title: Maven's Universal Artifact Addressing System
sections.content:
Maven coordinates (also called **GAV coordinates** for groupId, artifactId, version) are the unique address for any library or module in the Maven ecosystem. Think of them like a postal address: the **groupId** is the country and city (organization namespace), the **artifactId** is the street and house number (specific project), and the **version** is the apartment number (release).

For example, org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web:3.2.0 uniquely identifies one specific JAR file among millions. The groupId follows reverse-domain naming like com.company.product to ensure global uniqueness — your company owns that namespace just like it owns the domain. The artifactId names the specific module within that organization, like user-service or payment-api. The version follows semantic versioning conventions (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) to signal compatibility. Maven uses these coordinates to locate artifacts in repositories, resolve dependencies, and avoid naming conflicts. When you declare a dependency, Maven searches repositories using the coordinate path: groupId becomes directories, artifactId is the folder, version is the subfolder.

sections.title: GAV Coordinates
sections.content:
amber|groupId|~Organization namespace|reverse domain|org.springframework|prevents collisions
blue|artifactId|~Module name|spring-core|becomes the JAR name|unique within group
emerald|version|~Release number|MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH|1.0.0 or 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT|semantic versioning
violet|Maps to a path|~Repo lookup|group becomes folders|then artifact, then version|artifact-version.jar

sections.title: Declaring Dependencies with Maven Coordinates
sections.content:
```xml
// pom.xml dependency section showing GAV coordinates
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>  // Organization namespace
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>  // Specific module
    <version>3.2.0</version>  // Release version
  </dependency>
  
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
    <version>8.2.0</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>  // Only needed at runtime, not compile time
  </dependency>
  
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
    <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
    <version>1.18.30</version>
    <scope>provided</scope>  // Compile-time only, not packaged
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

// These coordinates map to repository paths:
// org/springframework/boot/spring-boot-starter-data-jpa/3.2.0/spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-3.2.0.jar
```

sections.title: When Maven Coordinates Matter Most
sections.content: You interact with Maven coordinates every time you add a library to your project — searching search.maven.org or mvnrepository.com for the right GAV. **Multi-module projects** use coordinates to reference sibling modules: if order-service depends on common-utils, you declare com.company:common-utils:1.0.0 as a dependency. **Publishing your own library** requires choosing coordinates carefully — the groupId must match a domain you control (verified when publishing to Maven Central), and the artifactId should clearly identify the module's purpose. **Dependency version management** relies on coordinates: Spring Boot's parent POM defines versions for hundreds of artifacts by their groupId and artifactId, letting you omit version numbers in your dependencies. Understanding coordinates is critical when resolving **version conflicts** — Maven uses the nearest definition rule based on dependency tree depth.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using arbitrary groupId values**: Freshers often invent groupIds like my.project or test.app instead of reverse-domain names. This causes publication rejections and namespace collisions. Always use a domain you control: com.yourcompany or io.github.yourusername.
- **Confusing groupId with Java package names**: The groupId doesn't have to match your code's package structure. groupId is an organizational namespace for Maven artifacts, while packages organize Java classes. They often align by convention (org.springframework groupId with org.springframework.boot packages), but it's not required.
- **Forgetting that artifactId should be globally unique within groupId**: Two modules in your organization can't have the same artifactId even if they're in different Git repos — the groupId plus artifactId must uniquely identify the module across all your projects.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **GAV coordinates**: groupId, artifactId, and version together form a unique identifier for every Maven artifact worldwide
- **groupId namespace**: Uses reverse-domain notation (com.company.product) to ensure global uniqueness and prevent naming collisions between organizations
- **artifactId specificity**: Names the specific module or library within the groupId namespace, like spring-core or user-service
- **version semantics**: Follows MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format where major changes break compatibility, minor adds features, patch fixes bugs
- **Repository paths**: Coordinates map directly to filesystem paths in Maven repositories: groupId/artifactId/version/artifactId-version.jar
- **Dependency declaration**: Every dependency in pom.xml requires groupId, artifactId, and usually version (can be inherited from parent POM)
- **Search and discovery**: Tools like search.maven.org and mvnrepository.com let you search by name and copy coordinates for any public library

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven coordinates are the unique identifier for any library or module in the Maven world. They're written as three parts: groupId colon artifactId colon version, like org dot springframework dot boot colon spring-boot-starter-web colon 3.2.0. The groupId is the organization namespace using reverse-domain format — it's like the publisher of the library. For example, org dot springframework means it's published by the Spring team. The artifactId is the specific module name within that organization, so spring-boot-starter-web is one particular library they publish. The version is the release number following semantic versioning. When you add a dependency to your pom dot XML, you specify these three pieces and Maven uses them to find and download the right JAR file. The coordinates solve a critical problem: two different companies could both have a library called utils, but com dot google colon utils and com dot company colon utils are completely different artifacts that won't collide. Maven converts coordinates into file paths — the groupId becomes nested directories, then artifactId, then version. One mistake freshers make is using random groupIds like my dot project instead of proper reverse-domain names. When you publish to Maven Central, you have to prove you own that domain, so always use something like io dot github dot yourusername if you don't have a company domain.

questions.question: What is the difference between a SNAPSHOT version and a release version in Maven?
questions.title: SNAPSHOT vs Release Versions in Maven
questions.direct_answer: A SNAPSHOT version like 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT is a work-in-progress build that can change with every commit — Maven re-checks for newer snapshots on each build. A release version like 1.0.0 is immutable and permanently represents that exact code state — once published, that version number never changes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding Maven versioning semantics — SNAPSHOT behavior is a frequent source of confusion and build reproducibility issues
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Maven re-downloads SNAPSHOTs periodically or that release versions are cached forever and never checked for updates
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that production deployments must never use SNAPSHOT dependencies because they're non-reproducible — today's 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT could be different code tomorrow

sections.title: Maven's Two Versioning Models
sections.content:
Maven distinguishes between **SNAPSHOT versions** (development builds) and **release versions** (immutable artifacts) to support both active development and stable production deployments. A SNAPSHOT version like 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT signals that this code is still changing — it's a moving target that gets rebuilt frequently during development.

Maven treats SNAPSHOTs specially: it periodically checks remote repositories for newer snapshots with the same version number and updates your local cache. In contrast, a release version like 1.0.0 is permanent and immutable — once you publish 1.0.0, that version number is locked forever and always refers to the exact same bytecode. Think of SNAPSHOTs like a draft document that gets edited multiple times, while releases are the final published version sent to the printer. This distinction is critical for **build reproducibility**: if your project depends on a SNAPSHOT, rebuilding next week might pull different code even though the version number looks the same. Release versions guarantee that mvn clean install produces identical output every time.

sections.title: SNAPSHOT vs Release
sections.content:
amber|SNAPSHOT|~Work in progress|1.0.0-SNAPSHOT|can change anytime|re-checked on build
blue|Release|~Frozen forever|1.0.0|immutable bytecode|never re-downloaded
emerald|Update policy|~-U forces refresh|daily check by default|cached after first fetch|speed comes from cache
rose|Production rule|~Releases only|reproducible builds|no overnight surprises|never ship SNAPSHOTs

sections.title: Declaring SNAPSHOT vs Release Versions
sections.content:
```xml
<!-- development build: re-fetched as it keeps changing -->
<version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

<!-- release build: immutable forever once published -->
<version>1.0.0</version>
```
`mvn install -U` forces Maven to re-download the latest SNAPSHOT instead of using the cached copy.

sections.title: SNAPSHOT vs Release Version Behavior
sections.content:
| Aspect | SNAPSHOT Version | Release Version |
|---|---|---|
| Mutability | Changes frequently with new commits | Immutable forever once published |
| Maven update check | Re-checks repository daily or on demand | Never checks — uses cached version |
| Intended use | Active development and team integration | Production deployments and stable APIs |
| Reproducibility | Non-reproducible — same version different code | Fully reproducible — same version same bytecode |
| Publishing | Can overwrite existing SNAPSHOT repeatedly | Cannot republish same release version number |

sections.title: When to Use Each Version Type
sections.content: Use **SNAPSHOT versions** during active development when you're building features and need the latest code from your team. If you're working on a multi-module microservices project, the order-service module depends on common-utils:1.0.0-SNAPSHOT so it automatically picks up the latest shared code without constantly bumping version numbers. When you run mvn install, Maven publishes the SNAPSHOT to your local repository or company Nexus server, and teammates get updates on their next build. Switch to **release versions** when you're ready to deploy to production or publish a stable API. Change 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT to 1.0.0, run mvn deploy, then immediately bump to 1.0.1-SNAPSHOT for the next development cycle. Release versions guarantee that your production deployment uses the exact tested code — no surprises from overnight commits. Never use SNAPSHOT dependencies in production because they violate the principle of reproducible builds.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Deploying SNAPSHOT dependencies to production**: Freshers sometimes ship applications that depend on SNAPSHOT versions, creating a nightmare scenario where production behavior changes unpredictably because Maven silently pulls a newer snapshot with breaking changes. All production dependencies must be releases.
- **Not understanding Maven's SNAPSHOT update policy**: By default Maven checks for new SNAPSHOTs once per day, so freshers are confused when their build doesn't pick up the latest code their teammate just pushed. You need mvn clean install -U (uppercase U) to force an immediate update.
- **Reusing release version numbers**: After publishing 1.0.0 to Maven Central, freshers try to republish the same version with bug fixes. Maven Central rejects this because release versions are immutable. You must increment to 1.0.1 for any code change.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **SNAPSHOT mutability**: SNAPSHOT versions can change without the version number changing — Maven periodically fetches the latest build from repositories
- **Release immutability**: Release versions are permanent and frozen — 1.0.0 always means the exact same bytecode forever
- **Update policy**: Maven checks for SNAPSHOT updates daily by default — use -U flag (mvn install -U) to force immediate update
- **Build reproducibility**: SNAPSHOT dependencies violate reproducible builds because today's 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT could differ from tomorrow's
- **Development workflow**: Teams use SNAPSHOTs during feature development and switch to releases for production deployment
- **Version lifecycle**: Typical flow is 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT development, release 1.0.0, immediately bump to 1.0.1-SNAPSHOT for next cycle
- **Production rule**: Never use SNAPSHOT dependencies in production — they're non-deterministic and make debugging impossible when behavior changes mysteriously

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A SNAPSHOT version is a work-in-progress build that can change without the version number changing. If your dependency is 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT, Maven will periodically check if there's a newer build with that same version number and download it. This is useful during development when your team is actively working on code — you want the latest changes without constantly bumping version numbers. A release version like 1.0.0 is the opposite — it's immutable and permanent. Once you publish 1.0.0, that version number is locked forever and always represents the exact same bytecode. Maven caches release versions and never checks for updates. The key difference is reproducibility. If I build my app today with a SNAPSHOT dependency, and you build it tomorrow, we might get different code even though we're using the same version number. With release versions, we're guaranteed to get identical results. In practice, you use SNAPSHOTs during feature development so teammates automatically get each other's latest code. When you're ready to deploy to production, you change the version to a release like 1.0.0, deploy it, then immediately bump to 1.0.1-SNAPSHOT for the next development cycle. A critical mistake freshers make is deploying apps with SNAPSHOT dependencies to production. That's dangerous because your production behavior could change overnight when someone commits new code. All production dependencies must be release versions for predictable, reproducible deployments.

questions.question: What is the standard Maven project directory structure?
questions.title: Maven Standard Directory Structure
questions.direct_answer: Maven's standard directory structure puts Java source code in src/main/java, test code in src/test/java, configuration resources in src/main/resources and src/test/resources, and compiled output in the target/ directory. This convention means every Maven project has the same predictable layout.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Maven project navigation — knowing where to put code, tests, and resources is fundamental for any Java backend work
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing where to put application.properties or other config files — they go in src/main/resources, not in the java directory
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Spring Initializr generates this structure automatically and that target/ is in .gitignore because it's generated output, not source code

sections.title: Maven's Convention-Based Project Layout
sections.content:
Maven enforces a **standard directory structure** that every Java developer recognizes instantly, eliminating the "where does this file go?" question. The structure separates source code, test code, resources, and build output into well-defined locations. **src/main/java** contains your production Java source files organized by package structure. **src/test/java** holds your JUnit test classes, mirroring the same package hierarchy. **src/main/resources** stores configuration files like application.properties, XML configs, SQL scripts, and static assets that get packaged into your JAR. **src/test/resources** contains test-specific configs and data files.

All compiled bytecode, packaged JARs, and build artifacts land in the **target/** directory, which is temporary and regenerated on every build. This convention means when you clone any Maven project, you immediately know where everything lives without reading documentation. IDEs like IntelliJ IDEA automatically recognize this structure and mark directories correctly — src/main/java as source roots, src/test/java as test roots, target/ as excluded from version control.

sections.title: Standard Maven Layout
sections.content:
amber|src/main/java|~Production code|by package|your application|compiled to target/classes
blue|src/main/resources|~Config + assets|application.properties|static files, SQL|packaged into the JAR
emerald|src/test/...|~Tests + test config|mirrors main packages|JUnit classes|never in the prod artifact
violet|target/|~Generated output|classes + JAR|gitignored|wiped by mvn clean

sections.title: Complete Maven Project Directory Structure
sections.content:
```text
// Maven standard layout for order-service project
order-service/
├── pom.xml                          // Project configuration
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/                   // Production source code
│   │   │   └── com/company/order/
│   │   │       ├── OrderController.java
│   │   │       ├── OrderService.java
│   │   │       └── OrderRepository.java
│   │   └── resources/              // Config and static files
│   │       ├── application.properties
│   │       ├── data.sql           // Schema initialization
│   │       └── static/logo.png
│   └── test/
│       ├── java/                   // Test source code
│       │   └── com/company/order/
│       │       └── OrderServiceTest.java
│       └── resources/              // Test-specific configs
│           └── application-test.properties
└── target/                          // Generated output (not committed)
    ├── classes/                     // Compiled .class files
    ├── test-classes/
    └── order-service-1.0.0.jar      // Final packaged artifact
```

sections.title: When Maven's Structure Guides Your Decisions
sections.content: Follow Maven's conventions for **all production Java projects** unless you have a compelling reason not to — IDEs, build tools, and CI/CD pipelines expect this layout. **Spring Boot applications** always use this structure because Spring Initializr generates it by default, and Spring Boot's auto-configuration scans src/main/resources for application.properties. **Configuration files** like database connection properties or logging configs always go in src/main/resources, not scattered in random directories. **Static web assets** for serving HTML, CSS, or JavaScript belong in src/main/resources/static/ so Spring Boot's embedded server finds them. **Database migration scripts** for Flyway or Liquibase go in src/main/resources/db/migration/. The structure also clarifies what belongs in version control: commit everything under src/, exclude target/ in .gitignore since it's generated output. Multi-module projects nest this structure — each module is a self-contained Maven project with its own src/ and target/ directories.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Putting config files in src/main/java**: Freshers often create application.properties right next to their Java classes because that's where they're working. Resources must go in src/main/resources or they won't be included in the packaged JAR, causing "file not found" errors in production.
- **Committing the target directory to Git**: The target/ folder contains compiled bytecode and packaged JARs that are generated on every build. Freshers sometimes commit this 50MB directory, bloating the repository. Always add target/ to .gitignore — it's reproducible build output.
- **Creating custom directories like src/code or lib/**: Fighting Maven's conventions by making up your own structure leads to hours of Maven configuration to tell it where to find things. Just follow the standard — every Java developer already knows it and every tool supports it natively.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **src/main/java**: Production Java source code organized by package structure — this is where your application code lives
- **src/test/java**: JUnit and other test classes mirroring the production package hierarchy for unit and integration tests
- **src/main/resources**: Configuration files (application.properties), static assets, database scripts — anything non-Java that gets packaged
- **src/test/resources**: Test-specific configuration files and test data that shouldn't be included in production builds
- **target/ directory**: Generated output containing compiled classes, packaged JARs, test reports — always excluded from version control via .gitignore
- **Package mirroring**: Test classes in src/test/java should mirror the package structure of src/main/java for clarity and organization
- **IDE recognition**: IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, and VS Code automatically detect Maven structure and mark directories correctly without manual configuration

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven uses a standard directory structure that's the same across all projects. Your production Java code goes in src slash main slash java, organized by package structure just like normal Java packages. Test code goes in src slash test slash java, usually mirroring the same package hierarchy as your main code. Configuration files like application dot properties, database scripts, or static web assets go in src slash main slash resources. That's important — resources is for anything that's not Java source code but needs to be packaged into your JAR. There's also src slash test slash resources for test-specific configs. Everything gets compiled and packaged into the target directory, which is generated output that you never commit to Git. For example, in a Spring Boot order service, you'd have OrderController dot java in src slash main slash java slash com slash company slash order, and the application dot properties config file would be in src slash main slash resources. When you run mvn package, Maven compiles everything and creates order-service-1.0.0 dot jar in target. One common mistake freshers make is putting application dot properties in the java directory instead of resources. That file won't be included in your JAR and you'll get file not found errors when you deploy. Another mistake is committing the target folder to Git — that's generated output that should be in your gitignore file. The beauty of this structure is that every Maven project looks identical, so when you join a new team or work on open source, you instantly know where everything is.

questions.question: What is Maven Central and how does Maven use it?
questions.title: Maven Central Repository
questions.direct_answer: Maven Central is the default public repository at repo1.maven.org and search.maven.org containing virtually every open-source Java library. When you declare a dependency in pom.xml, Maven automatically searches Maven Central, downloads the artifact, and caches it in your local repository at ~/.m2/repository for reuse.

sections.title: Maven Central: The Universal Java Library Repository
sections.content:
Maven Central is the default public repository that hosts virtually every open-source Java library in existence — it's like npm for JavaScript or PyPI for Python, but specifically for the Java ecosystem. Located at repo1.maven.org and searchable at search.maven.org, Maven Central contains millions of artifacts from Spring Framework to Apache Commons to Google Guava. When you declare a dependency in pom.xml, Maven automatically queries Maven Central using the artifact's GAV coordinates, downloads the JAR file, and stores it in your **local repository** at ~/.m2/repository (on Linux/Mac) or C:\Users\YourName\.m2\repository (on Windows). This local cache is critical: Maven checks it first before hitting the network, so you're not re-downloading Spring Boot on every build.

Think of it as a three-tier system: your pom.xml declares what you need, Maven checks the local cache, and if not found, it fetches from Maven Central and caches locally. Companies often run **internal repositories** like Nexus or Artifactory that sit between developers and Maven Central, caching artifacts and hosting private libraries.

sections.title: How Maven Resolves Dependencies from Maven Central
When Maven Central and Local Cache Matter
sections.content: **Every Maven build** uses Maven Central implicitly — unless you've configured custom repositories, Maven Central is where your dependencies come from. Understanding the local cache at ~/.m2/repository helps when **troubleshooting corrupted downloads**: if a build fails with checksum errors, delete that artifact's folder from ~/.m2/repository and re-run the build to force a fresh download. **Corporate environments** usually configure a **repository manager** like Nexus between developers and Maven Central to cache artifacts locally, enforce security scans, and host proprietary libraries. When searching for libraries, **search.maven.org** or **mvnrepository.com** let you find coordinates by name and see usage statistics, latest versions, and transitive dependencies. **Publishing open-source libraries** requires deploying to Maven Central via Sonatype OSS hosting, which involves proving domain ownership, GPG-signing JARs for security, and meeting quality requirements like having source and javadoc JARs.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking Maven downloads on every build**: Freshers are confused when builds work offline or run instantly after the first build. Maven caches everything in ~/.m2/repository and only downloads missing artifacts. This saves bandwidth but can cause stale dependency problems if the cache gets corrupted.
- **Not knowing how to clear the local cache**: When dependency problems occur, freshers reinstall Maven instead of simply deleting the problematic artifact folder from ~/.m2/repository. You can manually delete specific folders or use mvn dependency:purge-local-repository for a complete refresh.
- **Assuming all artifacts are on Maven Central**: Some commercial libraries (like Oracle JDBC drivers historically) aren't published to Maven Central for licensing reasons. You have to download manually and install to your local repository with mvn install:install-file, which freshers find confusing when the dependency can't be found automatically.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Maven Central location**: Primary repository at repo1.maven.org, searchable at search.maven.org and mvnrepository.com for finding library coordinates
- **Local repository cache**: Maven downloads artifacts to ~/.m2/repository (Linux/Mac) or C:\Users\YourName\.m2\repository (Windows) for reuse
- **Resolution sequence**: Maven checks local cache first, then queries Maven Central only if artifact is missing — avoids redundant network requests
- **Transitive dependencies**: Maven downloads not just your declared dependencies but also their dependencies recursively, all from Maven Central
- **Repository managers**: Enterprises use Nexus or Artifactory to cache Maven Central, host private artifacts, and enforce security policies
- **Publishing requirements**: To deploy to Maven Central, you need Sonatype OSS account, domain verification, GPG signature, source/javadoc JARs, and valid POM
- **Offline builds**: Once artifacts are cached locally, Maven can build without internet access using mvn install -o (offline mode)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven Central is the default public repository where virtually all open-source Java libraries are hosted. It's at repo1 dot maven dot org, and you can search it at search dot maven dot org to find libraries and their GAV coordinates. When you add a dependency to your pom dot XML, Maven automatically queries Maven Central using those coordinates, downloads the JAR file, and saves it to your local repository. The local repository is a cache directory on your machine at tilde slash dot m2 slash repository on Mac and Linux. This is important because Maven doesn't re-download dependencies on every build — it checks your local cache first. So the first time you build a Spring Boot project, Maven downloads Spring JARs from Maven Central and caches them locally. Every build after that uses the cached versions and runs much faster. The directory structure in your local cache mirrors Maven Central: groupId becomes nested folders, then artifactId, then version, then the actual JAR file. For example, Spring Boot starter web would be at org slash springframework slash boot slash spring-boot-starter-web slash 3.2.0. One common mistake freshers make is thinking Maven re-downloads everything on every build and wondering why their builds are slow. Actually, the slowness usually comes from Maven checking for SNAPSHOT updates or running tests, not from downloading. If you have corrupted downloads, you can delete that specific folder from dot m2 slash repository and Maven will re-fetch it. In companies, there's often an internal Nexus or Artifactory server that sits between you and Maven Central, caching artifacts for the whole team and hosting private company libraries that can't be public.
